newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. mission denies Taiwan visa cover-up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mission denies Taiwan visa cover-up.

text.p: A U.S. envoy flatly denied on Tuesday that Washington's de facto embassy in Taipei had tried to cover up a sex-for-visas scandal, saying there was no rape nor corruption as alleged by a former official.
Darryl Johnson, director of Washington's unofficial outpost, the American Institute in Taiwan, acknowledged that two cases of misconduct had been investigated and subsequent action taken.
"There is no scandal. There is no cover-up. We always try to maintain the highest standard of conduct at AIT," Johnson told reporters at a Taipei news conference.

Allegations by James Wood, ousted chairman of the institute's Washington office, that staff extorted sex and money from visa applicants swept Taiwan at the weekend and one former employee said he had evidence to support the charges.
The institute represents American interests in the absence of diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
Johnson said there was no coercive sex or rape, nor had the institute nor any institute individual embezzled money.

"The only case of such allegation we were aware of dated back to 1989. A woman who had applied for an immigrant visa from AIT charged that an AIT local national employee had made unwanted sexual advances," Johnson said.
"AIT investigated the case immediately. The employee denied the charge and he subsequently retired. As far as we know that woman never pursued this matter" in court, Johnson said.
Johnson declined to say whether the employee was dismissed because of the charges.
The employee on Tuesday told state television he was innocent, but refused to elaborate.
Johnson dismissed as baseless Wood's allegations that institute staff took bribes and that US$5.3 million in visa fees was missing.
He said the so-called missing funds were due mainly to accounting differences.
"There has been no rip-off. There however has been an ongoing internal dispute over accounting methods for a portion of AIT visa fees," he said.
He said the information underlying Wood's charges appeared to have come from another former AIT employee, Alex Keng.
He said Keng was dismissed in 1990 "for official misconduct" and that internal investigations determined Keng's information to be unfounded.
"Mr Keng's accusation was investigated several years ago and was determined not credible," he said.
Taiwan government officials have declined to comment.
Wood had said he was forced from his job when he tried to shed light on what he called widespread corruption at the institute.
Justice Minister Liao Cheng-hao told state radio that if the victim of sexual harrassment did not bring charges it would be unlikely the judiciary could do anything.
